title: On the phone and on video calls
topic: professional spoken exchanges; spelling out names and addresses
why: Phone calls and video meetings are where a foreign language gets truly tested. This lesson gives you the fixed phrases of a professional call, the French alphabet for spelling names and email addresses, and the vocabulary of video calls, building on the pronouns you already know.

{"lessons": ["

On the phone

Phone calls are hard in a foreign language: no gestures, no lips to read, and set phrases that go fast. The good news is that professional calls in French always use the same handful of formulas.

FrenchEnglish
Allô ?Hello? (only on the phone)
Agence Garonne, bonjour !Garonne Agency, good morning!
Je voudrais parler à Madame Fabre, s'il vous plaît.I'd like to speak to Ms. Fabre, please.
C'est de la part de qui ?Who's calling, please?
Ne quittez pas.Hold on, please. (don't hang up)
Je vous la passe. / Je vous le passe.I'll put you through to her / to him.
Elle est en réunion. / Il est en ligne.She's in a meeting. / He's on another call.
Voulez-vous laisser un message ?Would you like to leave a message?
Je lui transmets votre message.I'll pass on your message to him / her.
Je vous rappelle. / Elle peut me rappeler ?I'll call you back. / Can she call me back?

Notice the pronouns from unit 10: in Je vous la passe, vous is “to you” and la is Madame Fabre (“I pass her to you”). Vous comes before la because me, te, nous, vous always come before le, la, les; both go before the verb. For a man: Je vous le passe.

Allô is only for the phone: never use it to greet someone in the street. A company answers with its name + bonjour, and you answer with Bonjour + who you are: Bonjour, Karim Benali, de la société Duval.

Ne quittez pas literally means “don't leave”: it's the fixed phrase for “please hold”. And rappeler doubles its l like appeler: je vous rappelle, but nous vous rappelons.

", "

Spelling it out

You will constantly be asked to spell your name: Vous pouvez épeler, s'il vous plaît ? The French alphabet uses the same letters as English, but several of them sound confusingly different.

lettersounds liketrap for English speakers
A“ah”not “ay”
E“euh”not “ee”
I“ee”not “eye”
G“zhay”sounds like an English J
J“zhee”sounds like an English G
H“ash”ache
R“air”, from the throaterre
Uthe French u (lips rounded)different from ou
W“doo-bluh-vay”double vé
Y“ee-grek”i grec

The usual pairs to watch: G / J, E / I, and A / R. When spelling, add the extras: e accent aigu (é), e accent grave (è), e accent circonflexe (ê), c cédille (ç), deux l (ll), tiret (hyphen), majuscule (capital).

Héloïse : H, E accent aigu, L, O, I tréma, S, E.Héloïse: H, E acute accent, L, O, I with a dieresis, S, E.

Email addresses and phone numbers

For an email address: arobase (@), point (.), tiret (-), tiret du bas (_), and tout attaché (all one word).

karim.benali@duval.fr : karim point benali arobase duval point frkarim.benali@duval.fr

French phone numbers have ten digits, read in pairs: 06 42 17 85 30 is zéro six, quarante-deux, dix-sept, quatre-vingt-cinq, trente. A number starting with 06 or 07 is a cell phone.

When people spell on the phone, they often add a first name to avoid confusion: B comme Bernard, N comme Nicolas. Use it for your own name if the line is bad.

", "

Video calls, messages and appointments

Meetings on video have their own little phrases, often in the tu form among colleagues.

FrenchEnglish
Vous m'entendez ? / Tu m'entends ?Can you hear me?
Je vous entends mal.I can't hear you well.
Ça a coupé.We got cut off. / It cut out.
Ton micro est coupé.Your mic is muted.
Tu partages ton écran ?Can you share your screen?
Pouvez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît ?Could you repeat that, please?
La connexion est mauvaise.The connection is bad.

Note entendre mal: French puts the adverb after the verb, where English says “I can't hear you well”. French also drops “can” with verbs of perception: Je vous entends = I can hear you.

Leaving a message

On a messagerie (voicemail), keep the order: who you are, why you're calling, how to call back.

Bonjour, c'est Karim Benali, de la société Duval. Je vous appelle au sujet du devis. Vous pouvez me rappeler au 06 42 17 85 30. Merci, bonne journée !Hello, this is Karim Benali from Duval. I'm calling about the quote. You can call me back at 06 42 17 85 30. Thanks, have a nice day!

Setting an appointment

Vous êtes disponible jeudi ? — Jeudi à 10 h, ça vous va ? — Parfait, c'est noté.Are you free on Thursday? — Thursday at 10, does that work for you? — Perfect, I've made a note of it.

On the phone, the 24-hour clock is normal for appointments: à quatorze heures trente (2:30 p.m.). Repeat the time to confirm: Donc jeudi, quatorze heures trente.
